content:
Apple has responded to OpenAI's motion opposing its request for expedited discovery in an ongoing trade secrets lawsuit. Here are the latest developments.

Background

Earlier this month, Apple filed a lawsuit against a former employee, OpenAI, and io Products, alleging misappropriation of trade secrets and requesting expedited discovery.

The requests include early production of documents and communications, forensic imaging of devices and accounts, and early depositions of key witnesses outside of court.

In short, Apple wants substantive responses to written discovery requests within 30 days and a corporate representative deposition of OpenAI within 50 days—both earlier in the case rather than waiting for the broader fact discovery phase.

Below is an excerpt from Apple's motion:

The day before filing the motion, Apple also sought a temporary restraining order to bar OpenAI and other defendants from accessing, using, or disclosing what Apple claims is its proprietary information during the pendency of the case.

Apple's core argument is that the longer OpenAI and other defendants are allowed to use what it claims are trade secrets, the harder it will be to undo the damage.

Apple said:

After Apple filed the expedited discovery motion, OpenAI and other defendants immediately filed opposition briefs, arguing that the requests are unnecessary because the general discovery timeline already substantially overlaps with Apple's proposed expedited schedule. They also criticized Apple's requests as "overbroad," "unduly burdensome," and made for an "improper purpose."

Below is an excerpt from the opposition brief:

Speaking of which, that brings us to today's latest development.

Apple Fights Back

Apple today filed its reply to OpenAI's opposition brief, emphasizing that it has established "good cause for expedited discovery" in its initial papers and noting that even if expedited and general discovery overlap, its requests are no less meaningful for it.

Apple also pointed out that the opposition brief "has already suggested another possibility: that unless the Court orders otherwise, they will lodge objections, drag out discovery, and condition production of the misappropriation investigation on unrelated 'reciprocity' demands."

Below is an excerpt from Apple's latest filing:

In its reply, Apple also narrowed the time range for document requests to August 1, 2023 and later, while pushing back against OpenAI's earlier objection that the requests lacked date limits:

Finally, Apple reiterated that its urgency stems from concerns that OpenAI and other defendants may continue to use the trade secrets at issue while developing their own hardware, while Apple would have to wait "months or even years" to depose key witnesses:

Apple's motion for expedited discovery will be heard on October 1 before Judge Edward Davila, who may also rule on the requests before the hearing.
